lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-52800 for the First Phase of the Coastal Embankment Improvement Project (P128276). US$375 million approved 26 June 2013. The credit disbursed US$311.84 million. Original closing was 31 December 2020; actual closing was 31 December 2023. The original total project cost of US$400 million was cut to US$375.74 million after US$24.26 million of the credit, or SDR 18.223 million, was cancelled 17 days before closing. The scope was cut from 17 polders to 10 in January 2020. Environmental category A. The implementing agency was the Bangladesh Water Development Board. The project financed land acquisition and the resettlement and rehabilitation of people adversely affected by it (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2024; IEG ICR Review ICRR0024220, 30 November 2024).

lenders.name: Pilot Program for Climate Resilience, Strategic Climate Fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-14713 of US$25 million alongside the IDA credit; US$24,999,892.29 disbursed. Total disbursement across the credit and the grant was US$336.84 million as of 15 May 2024 (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2024).

cases.community: The project raised and widened embankments around coastal polders, which required private land and moved people living on the existing embankments. At appraisal the census survey of February 2012 found the first works package alone would affect 6,203 households and persons in their homes, places of business and other assets, plus 184 common resource structures, most of them on the existing embankments. The completion report states that by project close the project had made significant progress on land acquisition and compensation payments and that no construction was carried out until the process was complete. It then records that as of April 2024, four months after the credit closed, land acquisition payment stood at 92.4 per cent. The ICR Review adds that the Bank task team put the figure at 94 per cent as of June 2024 and that there was no further update after that. The unpaid balance was attributed to incomplete embankment works, compensation amounts as small as BDT 345, about US$4.00, and missing proof of ownership, including unavailable mauza maps, khatians, transfer and succession documents and possession records, as well as disputed claims and parcels under court cases. Responsibility for finishing the payments was left after closing to the project's key focal point, the executive engineers of the Bangladesh Water Development Board's operation and maintenance divisions and the Deputy Commissioner offices of the districts concerned. The Bank task team told the Independent Evaluation Group that the interim government changed the district administrations, including the Deputy Commissioners responsible for land acquisition payment, several times. Under the first works package 291 female-headed households were affected by resettlement and under the second works package 478; the completion report says the women heading those households received relocation and resettlement benefits and a grant. Thirty-six grievance redress committees were set up across the first two packages and received 269 complaints by 31 December 2023, all of which were closed. The completion report also states that resettlement assistance for involuntarily displaced people without title was completed before works started on each section. Financial management shortcomings forfeited US$12.69 million of concessional IDA funding, made up of US$6.24 million from an undocumented designated account and US$6.45 million left undisbursed.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,325 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The nearest figure in the Bank's own documents is the appraisal count of 6,203 households and persons affected in the first works package, from the February 2012 census survey in the Project Appraisal Document. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
cases.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2023 with land acquisition payment incomplete. The Bank task team reported 94 per cent paid as of June 2024 and acknowledged no further update since that date. The completion report of 28 June 2024 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 November 2024 reached the same rating on a split evaluation.

The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of these payments was found. The 94 per cent is not in a document at all: the review attributes it to the Bank task team. No document found names the households still unpaid, says how many they are, or gives a count of people actually relocated. The 92.4 and 94 per cent figures are percentages of payment value or of parcels, which the documents do not define. The completion report also states that no construction was carried out until the land acquisition process was complete.
cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, forests, physical cultural property, involuntary resettlement and projects on international waterways. The policy on indigenous peoples was not triggered, because none of the people in the selected polders were found to be from tribal communities (Project Appraisal Document, 29 May 2013). Because the credit was to pay for land acquisition and resettlement costs, a memorandum was prepared seeking approval from the Bank's Regional Vice Presidency for the use of credit proceeds to reimburse those costs. A Social Management and Resettlement Policy Framework and a draft resettlement action plan for the first works package were disclosed on 15 February 2013, and the financing agreement required the borrower to carry out the project in accordance with that framework and the environmental management framework. The implementing agency was the Bangladesh Water Development Board, which prepared each plan, got the Bank's agreement, disclosed it locally and implemented it; 36 grievance redress committees were set up across the first two packages. No construction was to be carried out on a site until land acquisition and compensation there were complete (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2024).

cases.title: Shop Removals on the Shahi Guzargah, Walled City of Lahore
cases.place: Shahi Guzargah (Royal Trail), from Delhi Gate past the Wazir Khan Mosque and Shahi Hammam, Walled City of Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
cases.point: Wazir Khan Mosque on the Shahi Guzargah, the historic street the works ran along (OpenStreetMap point for the mosque)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-73800 for the Punjab Municipal Services Improvement Project (P083929). US$50 million approved 1 June 2006, loan agreement signed 5 June 2006. The completion report's financing table gives US$48.85 million disbursed, 97.70 per cent of appraisal, with the borrower contributing US$5.74 million against US$8.90 million at appraisal; its data sheet gives the disbursed amount as US$48.86 million. Closing was extended twice, by 23 months in the restructuring of 2 August 2010 and by a further 12 months to 30 November 2013. Component 2 financed the pilot works in the Walled City of Lahore, including the Resettlement Action Plan. The completion report of 19 May 2014 rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Substantial. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 2 June 2015 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, overall Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Significant and the quality of the completion report Unsatisfactory.

cases.community: The project paid for the first stage of rebuilding the Shahi Guzargah, a 1.6 km historic street through the Walled City of Lahore, together with the facades, street surfacing, water supply, sewerage, drainage and electrical network along it. Surveys for the Resettlement Action Plan found 147 shops, counting sub-units, that had to be removed completely, 732 more shops that would be affected temporarily along the Shahi Guzargah, and 264 encroachments onto public space, mainly kitchens and washrooms, in the 47 residential streets running off it. The plan records who held the 147 shops: 84 belonged to the Auqaf Department, 22 to the Municipal Corporation, 18 to informal occupants and 10 were privately owned; 28 of the shopkeepers were owners, 76 non-resident owners, 8 resident tenants, 11 non-resident tenants and 22 were in an 'others' category. It also counted 79 day-seller shops, 10 khokhas (kiosks), 2 tharas and 19 mixed cases among the temporary sellers who would have to be compensated, and 53 employees working in the shops, whose families the plan put at 371 people. The plan states that no person was to be affected through an impact on houses or residences; the impacts it counts are on business premises and livelihoods. Of the 147 shopkeepers, 50 were earning between Rs 5,000 and Rs 20,000 a month and 61 between Rs 21,000 and Rs 35,000. Payments were to be made by cross cheque through the Revenue Department, to people with documentary proof of ownership. Employees of permanently displaced shops were to get a one-off Rs 15,000 and employees of temporarily disturbed shops Rs 6,000. By closing, the completion report records that 147 shops and 264 encroachments had been removed and 732 shops had been given temporary support, after more than a thousand meetings with shopkeepers, traders and residents. At closing the facade work was 72 per cent complete and street surfacing 52 per cent, with the rest finished using Government of Punjab funds.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,153 for this project. That figure is the plan-stage estimate in the Resettlement Action Plan itself, which states: 'Based on 879 shops/owners of the property being affected from minor to severe degrees with average family size of 7 persons, there would be impact on 6153 persons due to the project implementation in the Pilot Project area.' It is an estimate of people affected, arrived at by multiplying affected shops by an assumed household size, and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 147 shops removed completely, 264 encroachments removed and 732 shops given temporary support. No Bank document found counts people or households relocated: the Resettlement Action Plan states that no person was to be affected through an impact on houses or residences.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 November 2013 with the street works unfinished and completed afterwards with provincial funds. The Independent Evaluation Group rated the resettlement work a successful pilot. No independent follow-up study of what happened to the 147 shopkeepers after removal was found.

cases.confidence_note: The counts of shops removed, encroachments removed and shops temporarily supported come from the Bank's own completion report, and the ownership, income and entitlement detail from the project's Resettlement Action Plan, which the borrower prepared. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of the removals was found. The aftermath is not on the record: no document found records how much was actually paid to the 147 shopkeepers or the 53 employees, whether any were relocated to new premises, or what their incomes were afterwards. A master plan for 173 replacement shops is mentioned in the plan but no document found says it was built. The plan's own breakdowns of the 147 do not sum to 147: the ownership-status categories come to 145 and the income bands to 141, and the plan does not reconcile them.
cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A, the category assigned partly because of the substantial resettlement expected in the cultural heritage component. Two instruments governed it: an Environmental and Social Management Framework used to screen the municipal grants, and a Resettlement Framework for the cultural heritage works, under which a Resettlement Action Plan was implemented in the Walled City (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 May 2014). The plan set the entitlement matrix on the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, OP 4.12, and ruled out compensation for anyone who moved onto the site after the cut-off date. It required that compensation be paid about one month before any shop, part of a shop or plot was taken, that no shop or plot be taken without full payment, and that where a claim was disputed the assessed amount be pledged in the affected person's favour until the dispute was decided. Money was to be deposited by the project with the Land Acquisition Collector, who paid the shopkeepers; the construction contractor could start work only after the project took the site over. The executing agency was the Sustainable Development of the Walled City of Lahore Project, with the Revenue Department responsible for assessment, payment and possession (Resettlement Action Plan, March 2010).

cases.community: The project upgraded dry-season roads and tracks to all-season standard and maintained highway and feeder roads, scaled up from about 297 km to 700 km of upgrading. Its social impacts were land acquisition leading to involuntary resettlement, loss of strips of land, loss of structures, disturbance and disruption of livelihoods, and loss of common property resources. Cash compensation was paid in full for 91 project-affected households, for 76 land parcels and 48 structures. For the remaining 24 households, holding 19 land parcels and 11 structures - 115 households across the report's two figures - compensation was still outstanding at closing because the households had not supplied the documents and clearance needed for payment. The money for 22 of those 24 households had been deposited at their district administration offices; for the other two, payment awaited a determination by the Compensation Determining Committee, after which the Department of Roads was to place the amount in an escrow account. Financial management was downgraded to moderately unsatisfactory in 2018-19, partly over non-compliance with contract terms on a 5 per cent mobilisation advance. One road under the project, Satbanjh-Jhulaghat, had its own Resettlement Action Plan in September 2007, which counted 73 affected households on that road alone, of which 7 were severely affected and about 5 were Dalit households among the vulnerable groups.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5,824 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 91 project-affected households paid in full and 24 still owed, 115 across its two figures, and the one road-level resettlement plan opened here counts 73 affected households on the Satbanjh-Jhulaghat road. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
cases.outcome: The credit closed on 15 January 2020 with compensation unpaid to 24 households. The completion report leaves the final payments to the district administration offices and the Compensation Determining Committee, and no later document found records whether they were made.

cases.title: Land and Structures Taken for the Swat Right-Bank Road
cases.place: Provincial highway S3-B, the Chakdara to Kanju section on the right bank of the Swat river, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
cases.point: Chakdara, the southern end of the 40.9 km of highway S3-B reconstructed under the project (OpenStreetMap town point)

lenders.name: World Bank, as administrator of the Multi Donor Trust Fund for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, FATA and Balochistan
lenders.role: Grants TF-10112, TF-15895 and TF-16992 for the MDTF KP Emergency Roads Recovery Project (P125584). Original commitment US$8.0 million, approved 23 August 2011 and effective 17 October 2011; first additional financing of US$9.1 million approved 15 January 2014 and second of US$9.0 million approved 30 May 2014; revised amount US$26.10 million and US$25.62 million disbursed. Closing ran from 30 June 2014 for the first phase to 31 October 2015 for the third. Category B. Trust fund money is not normally usable for compensation, so approval was sought and given to pay compensation for lost assets and lost production from the grant funds. The completion report of 11 August 2016 rated outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Satisfactory, and risk to development outcome Significant; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 February 2017 agreed on outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance and gave risk to development outcome as Substantial. The two documents also give different approval and closing dates: the completion report's data sheet gives approval of the first phase as 23 August 2011 and the last closing as 31 October 2015, while the Independent Evaluation Group's data sheet gives Bank approval as 16 July 2011 and actual closing as 12 December 2015. The completion report's own data sheet names the first grant TF-10112 in its header and TF-10122 in its key dates table; TF-10112 is the number the Independent Evaluation Group uses.

cases.community: The project reconstructed 40.9 km of provincial highway S3-B from Chakdara to Kanju on the right bank of the Swat river, plus link roads, after a military operation and floods. The road serves a population of about 300,000 people on the right bank. The section of the same highway from Kanju to Madyan was funded by USAID and is not part of this project. The project paper for the first phase estimated that 498 people would be directly affected, about 3.75 acres of land would be acquired with crop-loss compensation on a further 1.75 acres where farmers had encroached on the right of way, 1,000 trees would be lost and 158 structures affected. The completion report gives the outcome: in Phase I, 114 people were affected, 1.6 acres of land in all were acquired or reclaimed, 74 trees were lost and 24 structures. In Phase II, 88 people were affected, crops were lost over 4.5 acres, and 731 trees and 23 structures were lost. In Phase III, 12 people were affected with very small losses. Those three phase figures come to 214 affected people; the report gives no total of its own. The completion report states that 98 per cent of affected parties had been compensated by the time it was written; the remainder were absent and had not responded to efforts to reach them. Its own summary says 'virtually all persons who lost property were compensated'. It also records 'delays in compensation payment at times', and says that when the provincial highway authority pulled its Deputy Director for Environment and Resettlement out of the project management unit for five months there were delays in handling grievance cases and in paying compensation. The report adds that the provincial government appears reluctant to devote staff and resources to social and environmental compliance. Grievance redress committees made up of affected people dealt with disputes over land ownership, compensation and payment delays. Auditors engaged by the provincial highway authority reviewed all three phases and reported a high degree of compliance.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5,398 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts affected people phase by phase - 114, 88 and 12, 214 together - against 498 estimated for Phase I at the project-paper stage. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
cases.outcome: The last grant closed on 31 October 2015 with 2 per cent of affected parties uncompensated because they could not be found. The project's savings on compensation and land acquisition, which came in below the amounts provided for, were used to build additional lengths of road.

cases.community: The project built a power station at Siddhirganj, a gas pipeline to feed it and a transmission line to carry its output. The gas pipeline required permanent acquisition of 46.05 hectares of land and temporary requisition of 85.00 hectares along the alignment. In the paragraph on gas pipeline resettlement the completion report records 'a total of 1,501 entitled persons were affected by the Project'; 93 of them lost structures, one lost a poultry farm and one lost a pond, and 201 female-headed households were affected. People losing approximately 20 per cent of their assets were treated as vulnerable and put into a livelihood restoration programme of cash grants and skills training. Handover of the pipeline right of way was itself delayed: the Narayanganj and Cumilla district administrations began handing over land only in mid-May 2012. On the transmission line, people living on the planned right of way objected to the route because of its impact in dense residential areas. The line was moved. The old route would have affected 72 families on private and public land; the route chosen instead affected 19 families, most of them squatting on public land and on private agricultural or industrial land. Because government rules barred the power grid company from permanently acquiring private land, the private landowners on the line were not compensated for their land at all. They kept ownership and received only compensation for crops and related temporary losses during construction. Across the grid and pipeline works the completion report says over 20,000 project-affected households were compensated for permanent and temporary impacts to land, land use and crops or livelihoods. Noise and emissions from the plant were found to put a nearby school and its students at risk, and a new school building was built at a safe distance and handed to the Bangladesh Power Development Board.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4,444 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 1,501 entitled persons affected by the project, in its paragraph on gas pipeline resettlement, and 19 families affected by the transmission line route that was built, against 72 families on the route that was dropped. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
cases.outcome: The credits closed on 31 December 2019. The transmission line was rerouted after objections, cutting the families affected from 72 to 19. Private landowners along the line retained title but were never paid for the land itself. Resettlement and rehabilitation costs on the pipeline and grid components were borne outside the Bank's financing.

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered two safeguard policies: environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Cleared environmental and social assessments, environmental management plans and resettlement action plans were conditions of loan negotiations. Compensation was set by the national Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982 together with the Bank's resettlement policy, OP 4.12, and both the amounts due under national law and any amounts payable above them were to be funded by the two implementing companies, Gas Transmission Company Limited and Power Grid Company of Bangladesh, rather than by the credit. Losses were to be assessed by a Compensation Determination Committee including a representative of the affected people and of an NGO; the company was then to deposit the money with the Deputy Commissioner of the district, who paid landowners by account payee cheque. cases.community: The project widened and strengthened eight road corridors and rehabilitated three more added at the September 2018 restructuring: 60.4 km from Radhanpur to Chanasma, 66.8 km from Mehsana to Palanpur including a 5 km bypass at Mehsana, and 27 km from Vallabhipur to Ranghola. cases.community: At Dehlon, where the project built a bypass, one of the owners of a plot refused the compensation offered in May 2017 and filed a case in the High Court; a complaint had already gone to the Bank's Grievance Redress Service in December 2016. In April 2017 the contractors tried to start work on the plot and the Bank team insisted all work stop until compensation was settled. Soon after the project closed on 5 June 2017 the contractor went back onto the plot and finished building the bypass. The plaintiff did not appear at the High Court hearing of 31 January 2018 and the hearing was rescheduled for the end of March 2018. The Bank's task team leader told the Independent Evaluation Group that half of the co-owners have been paid, that the co-owner who complained is still pursuing the matter in the High Court, and that the matter has not been resolved. There was also a built harm from the drainage works: in 2009 the project team found that drains built in urban areas sat above the plinth level of the buildings next to them, blocking numerous commercial and residential entrances. The Independent Evaluation Group attributes this to weak monitoring and to the roads board's environment and social officers not being involved in two upgrading works, which were closed out without proper clean-up, rehabilitation or compliance reports, and to inadequate handling of the environmental management plan and work-site safety on the output and performance based road contract. The Bank team later arranged an assessment and an action plan to remedy it. At appraisal the project expected 112 people from 24 households to be marginally or temporarily affected on the rehabilitation roads with none displaced, and about 31 hectares of land to be acquired. For the upgrading roads the appraisal document gives two readings of the same impact: its main text says 4,731 people from 1,233 households would be affected at least temporarily with people from 197 households expected to be displaced, while its safeguards annex, para 10.9, says 4,731 persons would be affected from 831 households of which 1,233 would be displaced from 197 households. Both are appraisal expectations, not outcomes.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,977 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The appraisal document's main-text figure for people affected at least temporarily on the upgrading roads is 4,731, with people from 197 households expected to be displaced; its safeguards annex gives 1,233 as the number displaced instead. cases.killed_note: Two fatal workplace accidents happened in 2016. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records them in one sentence, citing para 66 of the completion report: 'there were two fatal workplace accidents in 2016 which were not reported to the Bank'. The Bank's team learned of them only after making a specific request to the Punjab Roads and Bridges Development Board in February 2017, and then met contractors, consultants and the board about construction zone safety and traffic management. No document opened states that the accidents happened on works financed by the project, names the dead, gives the dates or locations, says which contractor's works they occurred on, or records any compensation to their families. cases.outcome: The loan closed on 5 June 2017. The bypass across the disputed plot was completed after closing. The Bank's task team leader told the Independent Evaluation Group that half the co-owners have been paid, that the co-owner who objected has not been, and that the case continues in the High Court, with the team still following the matter up as of the review of 8 May 2018. lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-47980 for the Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project (P083780). US$300 million approved 5 July 2005 and effective 19 October 2005; US$290.87 million disbursed. Original closing 30 March 2011; actual closing 31 March 2014. The project was restructured twice: the completion report's text dates the restructurings to August 2009 and January 2012, while its own data sheet dates them to 1 July 2009 and 7 February 2012. It financed 110 sub-projects under the urban investment component as well as the Chennai urban transport sub-component, and paid rehabilitation and resettlement costs: under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, the completion report's cost table gives INR 137.22 million at appraisal for rehabilitation and resettlement together with shifting of utilities, against INR 191.2 million actually spent (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 September 2014; IEG ICR Review ICRR14687, 12 May 2015).

cases.community: Under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, 212 title holders and 337 non-title holders were affected, including the resettlement of five displaced families. The cost of private land acquisition and resettlement and rehabilitation assistance there was INR 132.32 million, about US$2.20 million, or 8.5 per cent of that sub-component's cost. Under the urban investment component, 110 sub-projects were carried out; private land acquisition was involved in only seven of them and resettlement in one. In all, 21 hectares of private land were acquired from 31 landowners, and about 45 hectares of government land were transferred, including 23 acres of temple land. The resettlement took place in Salem, where 65 squatter families were moved into multi-storied apartments. Total compensation and resettlement assistance for those eight sub-projects came to INR 30 million, 0.73 per cent of their cost. The completion report records instances of delays in paying compensation and resettlement assistance, later addressed after follow-up by the Bank team and the state's urban development fund. At loan closure all compensation and assistance had been paid, except that the 65 families moved into the Salem apartment had not been given title to their flats: under Tamil Nadu rules titles were to be issued in December 2014, at the end of a five-year stay. An end-term impact evaluation of the Salem families found their incomes up, because more family members were working, and their housing better, having moved from huts to built flats. The same evaluation recorded what was wrong: drinking water supply was erratic and flats on the upper floors got no water because of problems lifting it; allotment of flats took no account of the elderly, old and sick, some of whom were put on higher floors; and residents reported thefts and a lack of security. The families kept ties to where they had lived, still sending children to schools there, visiting doctors there and mostly still working there. A separate evaluation of the Chennai transport families found 75 per cent satisfied with the rate of compensation, which the report attributes to a consent award process for private land and payment for structures without depreciation; compensation money was mostly spent on improving houses, 40 per cent of it. Land availability was a running problem: about 16 of the more than 40 sites needed for urban sub-projects had to be changed, for reasons including objections from nearby residents and court cases over unclear land titles.

cases.community: The project upgraded and rehabilitated roads in Assam, 978 km by closing against a revised target of 1,000 km. At appraisal, social screening covered about 420 km of roads, with a census and socio-economic survey of the people in every structure and on all land within the corridor of impact for Phase I of the upgrading component. It financed gravity irrigation schemes in marshlands covering 3,324 hectares. The government of Rwanda financed all resettlement costs. cases.community: People farming and living in the marshlands lost crops, land, cattle sheds and houses. The resettlement implementation completion report for the project, prepared by the project's social safeguards team in July 2012 and disclosed by the Bank, states: 'The numbers of affected people due to the project activities in all the marshlands so far are 3,088 in total. These people had activities either in the marshlands where canals were constructed or in the areas to be flooded and some buildings (such as houses) were built in buffer zones. Therefore, the project had to construct 36 houses in total in terms of compensations.' The total paid in the resettlement process was Rwf 460,938,198. Thirteen resettlement action plans were prepared and carried out, the Bank's completion report says, for the Nyarubogo dam, the Nyarubogo irrigation channel, the Ntende-Rwagitima irrigation channel, the Ntende dam, the Kiliba dam, the Rugeramigozi dam, the Kinyegenyege marshland, Gisaya, Kibaya, Kinyogo, Muvumba V, the Muvumba VIII dam and the Muvumba VIII channels. At Muvumba 8, cattle farms were flooded by the dam and the people affected were given cash to buy other farms for their animals; the report says most of them lived by animal keeping. Houses were replaced in three ways: new houses built in grouped settlements known as imidugudu, with the project providing materials and technical support and the work done as community labour; cash to renovate a house the household already owned elsewhere; or materials to finish an unfinished house. Cattle sheds were paid for in cash after valuation. The report's own list of grievances includes delays in payment for some affected people, caused by long district payment processes; people who did not find their names on the compensation lists in their sectors and were paid only after the lists were checked again; dissatisfaction with the value put on crops and assets; burial grounds that had not been declared at valuation, whose owners agreed to be helped to move them off the project sites; and family land conflicts, after families could not agree whose name went on the plan, which were sent to the local courts. The project's own conclusion is that all compensation was completed and that affected people were better off than before.

cases.community: Two requests for inspection were filed over this loan, in 2010 and 2011, and a third in 2020. The 2011 request was brought by Bauyrzhan Isaliev of the non-governmental organisation National Analytical Information Resource on behalf of the organisation and 24 project-affected people, and concerned four places: Turkestan, Sairam, Yntymak and Temirlanovka. In Turkestan, two family members had built a commercial facility in 2008 and intended to open it in 2009. They were told in early 2009 that the road project required them to stop the venture and that they would be compensated. Compensation was not paid. The Panel team was told the dispute turned on paperwork showing the size of the plot and on the absence of technical certificates for the building, which could not be issued without a valid land title. Road works at the site were suspended. The requester told the Panel team he would file a fourth court application to settle his entitlements. In Sairam, eight people holding agricultural land on 49-year state leases said works began on their land before compensation agreements were concluded. Bank Management confirmed that a contractor had moved equipment onto private property and started works on land for which compensation was still disputed and had not been paid, describing the incursion as lasting about one day and involving some initial scraping and removal of topsoil. Management also observed that the requesters did not claim that any material harm resulted from the incursion and proposed no specific remedial measures. By the Panel's visit of 26 September to 1 October 2011, seven of the eight had been paid; the eighth said he had reached an agreement but believed he had accepted less than he was owed. The Panel found the entitlement matrix in the South Kazakhstan Region Resettlement Action Plan appeared to allow one year of lost future income while Kazakh law appeared to require all remaining years of the lease, and that requesters in Sairam said they had never seen the leaflet describing the plan. In Yntymak, a settlement stretching 5 km along the highway out of Shymkent, residents said the designer's stated 35 to 40 metre distance from road to houses was in fact 15 to 20 metres. Bank Management said it could not state whether an appropriate design could be achieved without further land acquisition and population displacement. On Temirlanovka, Management agreed with the requesters that the environmental impact assessment was largely generic and lacked site-specific information and analysis. Over the life of the loan several thousand grievances were handled, covering the quality of workers' accommodation, compensation, restoration of temporarily used land and requests for livestock pens; the Bank team told the Independent Evaluation Group on 29 August 2025 that no exact data on grievances was recorded. The completion report gives no count of households relocated.

cases.ecosystem: The project was environmental category A. Bank Management agreed in 2011 that the environmental impact assessment for the Temirlanovka bypass was largely generic and lacked site-specific analysis; requesters said the bypass would damage the Tugai floodplain forest and the Arys river ecosystem. The completion report records contractors with insufficient environmental staffing, inadequate health and safety practices at construction sites and worker accommodation, and delays in rehabilitating borrow pits. The completion report records that ancient burial sites were found along the Otar-Uzynagash section and documented by local archaeologists. The Bank's project team told the Independent Evaluation Group on 29 August 2025 that works were halted, archaeologists were engaged and the finds were transferred to a museum; that account is not in any project document.
cases.outcome: The 2011 Panel found the request eligible on all six criteria but did not recommend an investigation, noting that Management had shown action was being taken and that the requesters said their concerns were resolved or about to be resolved. A third request was filed on 24 December 2020 by four residents of Shakpak Baba village, Tulkubassiy district, who said eight houses were flooded in 2017 with material damage and only one household was compensated, that wells and a concrete irrigation canal no longer worked, that road accidents had risen and that a cattle crossing under the road was partly blocked with gravel debris. Management said the 2017 flooding followed general snowmelt and rainfall across Kazakhstan rather than the roadworks, and commissioned a hydrological study in January 2021. In its eligibility report of 13 April 2021 the Panel recommended no investigation, finding no plausible link between the project and the 2017 flood, the clogged wells or the lost irrigation water, no material increase in the accident rate at Shakpak Baba, and acceptable maintenance of the cattle crossing culverts, while noting weaknesses in consultation and disclosure. The Board approved that recommendation on 26 April 2021. The loan closed on 31 December 2024 with a 42 km section of the Otar-Uzynagash road still unfinished after the original contract was terminated.

Civil works for the airport component could not start until the land compensation was settled in January 2018, and all works and supervision for that component began only in May 2018. Under the road component the grievance mechanism received 69 cases. All were closed by project closing except three: two concerning a subcontractor's failure to pay suppliers, and one gender-based violence case. The supplier cases were closed after project closing, after the road administration asked the main contractor to require the subcontractor to pay. fields_add.community: The World Bank completion report adds that the local area development programme built more than 40 schemes at a cost of more than US$13.8 million, and that the standard of health and safety supervision during those works was in many cases poor. Seven people were killed during construction on the project, five on the hydropower plant works and two on the local area development programme works. At closing, in all three countries some of the finished buildings, including courts, markets and health centres, were still not in use because no staff had been assigned to run them, and many lacked operation and maintenance plans, funding for running costs and connections to electricity or water. A completion audit of the livelihood restoration programme, the second of two independent standard of living surveys, found that more than 70 per cent of project-affected people reported improved livelihoods. The social specialist on the project's independent panel of environmental and social experts resigned in 2019 and was not replaced. Undated reporting from Burundi by Ferdinand Mbonihankuye, supported by the Rainforest Journalism Fund and the Pulitzer Center, followed the transmission lines that carry 26 MW from Rusumo Falls to the Gitega, Kobero and Muyinga stations in Burundi: 417 pylons were planned, and a NELSAP assessment cited in the article puts the area cleared for towers and substations at at least 24,081 hectares. The article says the law entitles each household within a 15-metre radius of a pylon to a plot of equivalent size, and quotes people who were offered money instead and said it was too little to replace what they lost. Antoine Ndayisaba, a farmer in Mugutu village in Gitega province, said the 200,000 Burundian francs, about US$98, he received for a 15 by 15 metre pylon plot would not buy replacement land. The family of Antoine Kamwenubusa, a man in his sixties at the Ku Mazi urban centre in Nyabikere commune, Karusi province, refused the compensation and asked instead for plots the size of those they lost; a son said the family's banana plantations were decimated for the pylon work and the family's income fell. In Rwanda, Patricia Uwingabiye of Kirehe district said people in Nyankurazo used to grow sweet potatoes, beans and peas in the Rusumo marshes and can no longer reach those fields because of flooding from the Kagera River, and NELSAP's Gaspard Bikwemu put the loss of wooded savannah on Nyankurazo hill at about 10 hectares. In Tanzania, Jean Baraka Habonimana of Karagwe village said the water supply had got worse since the dam was built, and Rachid Mbaraka of Rusumo village said tap water was rationed to about once a week.
